sweep_summary: Two title-hit items for Uab Meto, neither of which gives a stress statement for the language. (1) Himmelmann 2018 (open access, Zenodo; already held by the project, re-read): an areal chapter on intonation whose data languages are Totoli, Waima'a and Papuan Malay; no mention of Meto/Dawan anywhere in the text; only the general §3.1 caution that reported penultimate 'stress' in the region may be phrase-level edge tones — silent on the catalog's classification. (2) Heston 2018 Diachronica (paywalled; abstract and landing page saved): diachrony of word prosody in Makalero and Fataluku (Papuan); not about Uab Meto; priority none. The catalog's fixed-strict penult coding (Steinhauer 1996a:224, stress on the lexical stem, usually its penult) stands; the best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Culhane 2018 p.9/p.58 (Amfo'an variety, held by the project from the prior check), which confirms penult-of-the-foot stress with pre-foot syllables and enclitics outside the domain and refines rather than supersedes the deciding source; Edwards 2020 p.111 gives the same penult rule for Amarasi (a separate glottocode).

new_statements.quote: p.9: "All lexical roots in Amfo'an are comprised of a foot, which is minimally CV́V; word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the foot. In Amfo'an, the prosodic word is minimally composed of a disyllabic foot ... extra material which is external to the foot, such as additional syllable or consonant, are dominated by the prosodic word. For example, maʔfénaʔ 'heavy' consists of one foot and one additional syllable." p.58: "enclitics are not prosodic words on their own, but are parsed with the host as one prosodic word. However, stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the host."

new_statements.locator: §1.5.2 'Syllable, foot and word', p.9; §3 p.58, ex. (117)
new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate stress computed on the foot/lexical root, not on the whole word: pre-foot syllables (maʔ-fénaʔ) and enclitics (m-tóti=koo, n-béti=kau) are outside the stress domain, so surface words can carry stress on the antepenult or, with a monosyllabic-plus-prefix shape, on the final syllable. This agrees with Steinhauer 1996a:224 (stress on the lexical stem, usually its penult; petrified-prefix stems final) and with Edwards 2020 §3.3.4 p.111 for the sister variety Amarasi (amar1273; held by the project at 'Stress in Amarasi falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word', with VVCV(C) words as the only exception). Confirms the catalog's fixed-strict penult coding with domain = stem/foot; refines it by making enclitic extrametricality explicit.

new_statements.quote: Known varieties of Uab Meto have the five vowels /i e a o u/.7 Word stress falls on the penultimate vowel. Vowel-initial words begin with a predictable glottal stop; /asu/ 'dog' → [ˈʔasʊ]. While all Uab Meto varieties appear to share the same phoneme inventory, the segments in each variety have different distributions and behaviors.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's penult coding (penultimate stress) and as the Culhane 2018 statement (penultimate syllable of the foot) and Steinhauer 1996 p.224. It is a cluster-wide summary statement without domain detail, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Culhane's foot/stem-domain refinement (pre-foot syllables and enclitics outside the stress domain); it is compatible with it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One sentence in the language-background section: word stress falls on the penultimate vowel, stated for all known Uab Meto varieties (the paper cites Ro'is Amarasi, Kotos Amarasi and Molo data throughout, with occasional Amfo'an, Kusa-Manea, Baikeno and Amanuban). The example /asu/ 'dog' → [ˈʔasʊ] shows initial (= penultimate) stress on a disyllable. The paper says nothing about the stress domain (stem vs. word), clitics, prefixes, or secondary stress; the rest of the article is historical segmental phonology and never returns to stress (no other hit for stress/accent/prominence/tone; 'penultimate' otherwise appears only in the *ə > e reflex statement, p.6x §3.4).
new_statements.exceptions: none mentioned; the statement is unqualified ('Word stress falls on the penultimate vowel'). Note the phrasing is 'penultimate vowel', not 'syllable', which matters in a language with VV sequences but is not elaborated.
new_statements.identity_note: Edwards 2016 treats Uab Meto as a language/dialect cluster (also called Dawan[ese], Timorese, Atoni) and states the stress rule for 'known varieties of Uab Meto' collectively; its data are mainly Kotos Amarasi (Koro'oto, desa Nekmese'), Ro'is Amarasi (Suit, desa Buraen) and Molo (Middelkoop's draft dictionary), with occasional Amfo'an (Naitbelak dialect), Kusa-Manea, Baikeno and Amanuban. The catalog entry is for Uab Meto as a whole; the existing Culhane 2018 statement is specifically Amfo'an.

sources.quote: No language-specific statement on Meto/Dawanese; only the general caution (§3.1) that penultimate 'stress' reported for Austronesian languages of Indonesia and East Timor may be phrasal rather than lexical. Glottolog's tagging of this chapter to uabm1237 does not reflect Meto data in the text.
sources.locator: §3.1 (searched full text for Meto/Dawan/Amarasi: no hits)
sources.note: Areal chapter on intonation and information structure; its data languages are Totoli, Waima'a and Papuan Malay (Sources, p.372). A full-text search for Meto/Dawan/Atoni/Amarasi/Amfo'an returns no hit, so it contains no statement about Uab Meto. Its only bearing is the general caution (§3.1) that reported penultimate 'stress' in Austronesian languages of Indonesia and East Timor may be a phrase-final edge tone rather than lexical stress. Glottolog's tagging of this chapter to uabm1237 does not reflect Meto data in the text.
